Sup A: asprey_2000_monod_kinetics · Statistical tools for optimal dynamic model building (Monod kinetics)
The model describes baker’s yeast fermentation in a fed-batch reactor, predicting biomass and substrate concentrations over time. It combines reactor component balances with a Monod-type rate law for substrate consumption; the biomass and substrate balances account for growth, dilution, biomass loss, and substrate supplied in the feed. The process is represented by adjustable dilution and feed-substrate concentration profiles, with specified initial concentrations. The paper demonstrates model checking and experiment design using simulated response data with added measurement error, rather than reported measurements from a physical reactor. The authors use the example to test identifiability, distinguish the Monod model from a Canoid alternative, and design experiments for model discrimination and improved parameter precision.
availability: The paper does not state that code or reusable data for the bioreactor model are available.
comparison: The paper compares the Monod model with a rival model using Canoid-type kinetics.
data: The paper identifies the measured quantities as biomass and substrate concentrations but does not state the measurement instrument or assay.
data: The worked parameter-estimation example uses simulated response data with homoscedastic normal error variance 0.04 for each response, not reported physical reactor measurements.
design: The model-discrimination design uses ten sampling times and five control-vector-parameterization intervals for each of the two inputs.
design: The model-discrimination experiment improves the reported divergence criterion from an initial value of 1.98 to an optimal value of 1.19 × 10⁵.
design: The optimized model-discrimination experiment lasts 40 h, and both responses are sampled at the same selected times.
distinguishability: Under the same test conditions, the Monod and Canoid models are reported as distinguishable, with a value of 0.339 exceeding the 0.004 threshold.
equipment: The paper gives no reactor volume or physical scale for the example.
fit: The lack-of-fit table reports values of 0.58 for the Monod model and 1.96 for the Canoid model, against a reference chi-square value of 26.3.
fit: The paper concludes that the Monod model is better suited to the simulated data based on multiresponse chi-square lack-of-fit analysis, although both candidate models describe the data statistically well.
identifiability: The paper tests structural identifiability over a 40 h horizon using a five-element piecewise-constant input parameterization and parameter values in [0.01, 0.98].
identifiability: Under that test, the reported identifiability objective is 1.166 × 10⁻⁶, below the 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ tolerance, and the paper concludes the tested model is globally identifiable.
kinetics: The model uses Monod-type kinetics for substrate consumption.
mechanisms: The biomass balance accounts for growth, dilution, and biomass loss, while the substrate balance accounts for consumption and dilution with the feed.
methods: The paper uses control vector parameterization to represent time-varying inputs, including piecewise-constant profiles in the bioreactor example.
methods: The paper's identifiability and distinguishability tests are formulated as optimization problems, including semi-infinite and max-min problems.
operation: The dilution factor is allowed to range from 0.05 to 0.20 h⁻¹.
operation: The initial biomass concentration can be chosen between 1 and 10 g l⁻¹.
operation: The initial substrate concentration is fixed at 0.01 g l⁻¹ and cannot be manipulated in the experiment design.
operation: The process has two time-varying controls: dilution factor and substrate concentration in the feed.
operation: The substrate concentration in the feed is allowed to range from 5 to 35 g l⁻¹.
parameters: The model has four estimated parameters, shown as θ₁ through θ₄ in the parameter-estimation results.
parameters: The paper reports parameter estimates and confidence intervals after the model-discrimination experiment, but does not specify the parameter-estimation algorithm or software.
precedents: For dynamic parameter-precision design, the paper discusses Espie and Macchietto (1989), Körkel et al. (1999), and Zullo (1991), and states that its work to date is based largely on Zullo’s criterion.
precedents: The dynamic model-discrimination criterion builds on the Hunter–Reiner approach, whose extension to dynamic experiments was first attempted by Espie and Macchietto (1989).
precedents: The robust optimal-design methods for dynamic experiments are described further in Asprey et al. (2000).
precision: For improving parameter precision, the paper applies an E-optimal design to the Monod model using the parameter estimates obtained after the discrimination experiment.
precision: The E-optimal criterion rises from 6.41 × 10⁻⁶ to 14.3 in the designed precision-improvement experiment.
precision: The paper reports that confidence intervals were reduced by an average of 23.0% after the sequentially designed precision-improvement experiment.
purpose: The Monod fermentation model serves as an example for demonstrating tools for dynamic model building and statistical verification, rather than as a standalone validated production model.
scope: The example demonstrates design over a maximum experiment duration of 40 h and within the stated ranges for inoculation, dilution, and feed substrate concentration.
states: The model has two concentration states, biomass concentration and substrate concentration, and both are measured responses.
structure: The example is a dynamic model with two differential component balances and an algebraic rate law.
structure: The model is expressed as reactor-level concentration balances, with no spatially distributed reactor description presented.
system: The model is for fermentation of baker’s yeast in a fed-batch reactor.

Sup B: bolton_2006_cake_standard_blocking · Combined models of membrane fouling: Development and application to microfiltration and ultrafiltration of biological fluids (Cake-standard blocking)
The combined cake-standard blocking model describes fouling of a membrane by both cake formation on its surface and pore constriction within the membrane. It predicts filtered volume over time during constant-pressure operation and pressure over time during constant-flow operation, using Darcy’s law and the two mechanisms’ effects on filtration resistance. The model has two fitted parameters and is formulated with algebraic relations rather than dynamic state equations. The paper tested combined fouling models using human plasma IgG filtered through a sterilizing-grade PVDF membrane and BSA filtered through a virus-retention membrane, under both constant-pressure and constant-flow conditions. The cake-standard model improved fits in some tests, but the authors present it as most applicable when the observed fouling is consistent with both mechanisms, rather than as a model that fits a broad range of fouling curves.
assumptions: The authors note that if the mechanisms become coupled during filtration, fitted parameters can represent average behavior over the run.
assumptions: The model treats cake formation and standard blocking as independent mechanisms that proceed throughout filtration.
availability: The paper does not report whether model code or the experimental data are publicly available.
equipment: The BSA virus-filtration tests used Viresolve 180, a PVDF composite membrane with a thin ultraporous layer over a thicker microporous layer.
equipment: The IgG sterile-filtration tests used nominally 0.22 μm Durapore PVDF membranes in stainless-steel holders.
feed: The BSA feed was prepared at 2.5 mg/mL in pH 7.2 PBS.
feed: The human plasma IgG feed was prepared at 10.0 mg/mL in pH 7.2 PBS.
fitting: For the constant-pressure IgG comparison, the authors fit only the standard-blocking parameter in the standalone standard model rather than refitting the initial flux.
fitting: Model fits were assessed by minimizing the sum of squared residuals, with each residual defined as the difference between a measured point and its model prediction.
formulation: For constant-pressure operation, the cake-standard model calculates filtered volume as a function of time, while for constant-flow operation it calculates pressure as a function of time.
formulation: The combined fouling models are derived from Darcy’s law.
formulation: The model uses two fitted parameters.
formulation: The paper’s closed-form constant-pressure solution is stated to apply when its intermediate parameter is not near 1 or −1; when one mechanism dominates, the corresponding individual model should be used.
formulation: The supplied model specification has no dynamic state variables; the paper presents time-dependent outputs through algebraic model equations.
formulation: When one mechanism dominates, the cake-standard model reduces to the corresponding cake-filtration or standard-blocking model.
measurement: Data were collected every second for one hour in the described constant-pressure setup.
measurement: The BSA results were reported as the average of five runs, with error bars showing one standard deviation.
measurement: The constant-pressure setup measured filtrate weight using a collection vessel and electronic balance with a load cell interfaced to a computer.
mechanisms: In the cake-standard model, the available membrane area remains constant over the run.
mechanisms: The model combines cake filtration, in which a surface cake adds resistance, with standard blocking, in which material constricts pores from within.
mechanisms: The standard-blocking mechanism represents particles accumulating on the walls of straight cylindrical pores.
operation: Constant-flow IgG filtration was run at 579 L/m² h through Durapore membranes.
operation: Constant-pressure IgG tests used a transmembrane pressure of 10 psi, and constant-pressure BSA tests used 30 psi.
operation: Five constant-pressure BSA experiments used 47 mm holders and continued until flux had fallen by 98% from its initial value of 3.58 × 10⁻⁴ m/s.
operation: Three constant-flow IgG experiments measured pressure over time while the feed was pumped through 47 mm membrane holders.
operation: Three constant-pressure IgG experiments used 13 mm holders and continued until flux had fallen by 95% from its initial value of 1.13 × 10⁻³ m/s.
performance: For constant-flow IgG, the cake-standard model fit less well than the cake-intermediate and cake-complete models, whose SSR values were 0.58 and 1.36.
performance: For constant-flow IgG, the cake-standard model had an SSR of 13.5, substantially below the standalone standard model’s SSR of 980.
performance: For constant-pressure BSA, the cake-standard model had an SSR of 6.27 × 10³, better than the four standalone fouling models but worse than the cake-complete and cake-intermediate models.
performance: For constant-pressure IgG, the standalone standard model fit about as well as the combined standard-and-cake model.
performance: For the constant-flow IgG and constant-pressure BSA fits, the authors found caking to be a major component of the cake-standard model’s fitted behavior.
prior work: The authors compare their combined models with Ho and Zydney 2000, describing their own models as less physically detailed but numerically simpler.
prior work: The earlier Ho and Zydney model used three fitted parameters and numerical integration for pressure-time or volume-time predictions.
prior work: The paper builds the combined model from established individual fouling laws associated with Grace 1956 and Hermia 1982.
scope: The cake-standard model improves fits mainly for curves between the predictions of its two component models and cannot fit the described complete-blocking curve shape.
scope: The cake-standard model is less useful than the cake-complete model for fitting a broad range of individual-model predictions.
scope: The cake-standard model is most applicable when the observed fouling is consistent with both cake formation and standard blocking.
use: The cake-standard model is presented as a candidate for interpreting filtration data when the combined mechanisms match observed fouling, rather than as the paper’s general-purpose model for membrane sizing.
validation: The paper evaluates fits against the reported filtration experiments but does not describe an independent validation dataset for the cake-standard model.
